IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used completely verbatim as keystrokes. Write commands exactly as you want them sent to the terminal:

On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary.

It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

- Do not include extra whitespace before or after the keystrokes unless it's part of the intended command
- Extra text before or after the JSON will generate warnings but be tolerated
- The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes and special characters within strings
- Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action

#!/bin/bash

# Firewall rule applier script
# Reads rules.conf and generates iptables commands
# Running in dry-run mode - writes to applied.log instead of executing

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
RULES_FILE="$SCRIPT_DIR/rules.conf"
OUTPUT_LOG="$SCRIPT_DIR/applied.log"

if [[ ! -f "$RULES_FILE" ]]; then
    echo "Error: rules.conf not found"
    exit 1
fi

# Clear output log
> "$OUTPUT_LOG"

echo "# Firewall rules applied at $(date)" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
echo "# Dry-run mode - showing what would be executed" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
echo "" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"

while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n "$line" ]]; do
    # Skip comments and empty lines
    [[ "$line" =~ ^[[:space:]]*# ]] && continue
    [[ -z "${line// }" ]] && continue

    # Parse default policies
    if [[ "$line" =~ ^default_input:[[:space:]]*(.+)$ ]]; then
        policy="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
        policy_upper=$(echo "$policy" | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]')
        echo "iptables -P INPUT $policy_upper" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
        continue
    fi

    if [[ "$line" =~ ^default_output:[[:space:]]*(.+)$ ]]; then
        policy="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
        policy_upper=$(echo "$policy" | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]')
        echo "iptables -P OUTPUT $policy_upper" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
        continue
    fi

    # Parse allow in state established,related
    if [[ "$line" =~ ^allow[[:space:]]+in[[:space:]]+state[[:space:]]+(.+)$ ]]; then
        states="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
        states_upper=$(echo "$states" | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]')
        echo "iptables -A INPUT -m state --state $states_upper -j ACCEPT" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
        continue
    fi

    # Parse allow in tcp PORT from CIDR/any
    if [[ "$line" =~ ^allow[[:space:]]+in[[:space:]]+tcp[[:space:]]+([0-9]+)[[:space:]]+from[[:space:]]+(.+)$ ]]; then
        port="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
        source="${BASH_REMATCH[2]}"
        if [[ "$source" == "any" ]]; then
            echo "iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport $port -j ACCEPT" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
        else
            echo "iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport $port -s $source -j ACCEPT" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
        fi
        continue
    fi

    # Parse deny in from CIDR
    if [[ "$line" =~ ^deny[[:space:]]+in[[:space:]]+from[[:space:]]+(.+)$ ]]; then
        source="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
        echo "iptables -A INPUT -s $source -j DROP" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
        continue
    fi

done < "$RULES_FILE"

echo "" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
echo "# End of rules" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"

echo "Rules applied successfully"
exit 0

steps.message:
Analysis: I found the problem! The issue is a classic firewall rule ordering problem. In rules.conf, the deny rule for 10.80.0.0/16 comes BEFORE the allow rule for 10.80.4.0/24. Since 10.80.4.0/24 is a subnet within 10.80.0.0/16, the broader deny rule matches first and drops the traffic. The conn.log confirms this - traffic from 10.80.4.17 is being matched by the 'deny in from 10.80.0.0/16' rule and dropped. The monitoring subnet rule exists but never gets evaluated because the deny rule catches the traffic first. Additionally, I notice apply.sh is in dry-run mode - it only writes to applied.log instead of actually executing iptables commands.
Plan: I need to fix the rule ordering in rules.conf by moving the more specific allow rule for 10.80.4.0/24 BEFORE the broader deny rule for 10.80.0.0/16. This way, monitoring traffic will be allowed before the broader block is evaluated. Firewall rules are processed in order, and the first match wins.

        policy="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
        policy_upper=$(echo "$policy" | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]')

        states="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
        states_upper=$(echo "$states" | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]')
        exec_iptables "iptables -A INPUT -m state --state $states_upper -j ACCEPT"
        continue
    fi

    # Parse allow in tcp PORT from CIDR/any
    if [[ "$line" =~ ^allow[[:space:]]+in[[:space:]]+tcp[[:space:]]+([0-9]+)[[:space:]]+from[[:space:]]+(.+)$ ]]; then
        port="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
        source="${BASH_REMATCH[2]}"
        if [[ "$source" == "any" ]]; then
            exec_iptables "iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport $port -j ACCEPT"
        else
            exec_iptables "iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport $port -s $source -j ACCEPT"
        fi
        continue
    fi

    # Parse deny in from CIDR
    if [[ "$line" =~ ^deny[[:space:]]+in[[:space:]]+from[[:space:]]+(.+)$ ]]; then
        source="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
        exec_iptables "iptables -A INPUT -s $source -j DROP"
        continue
    fi

done < "$RULES_FILE"

echo "" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"
echo "# End of rules" >> "$OUTPUT_LOG"

echo "Rules applied successfully"
exit 0
EOFSCRIPT
